items.prose: With a block of 3, every letter of a name and its end mark is one row.
items.question: How many rows does isabella give?

feedback.correct: 9: eight letters and the end mark.
feedback.generic: Not quite. One row per letter plus one.

byKey.no-end: You left out the row whose target is the end mark.

explain.text: isabella has 8 letters, so it gives $8 + 1 = 9$ rows.

items.prose: With `.` as 0 and a to z as 1 to 26, take the name olivia and a block of 3.
items.question: Which context predicts the v?

options.why: That context, `.ol`, predicts the first i.
That is the context of the second i, after l, i and v.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the three symbols just before v.

explain.text: Before v come o (15), l (12) and i (9), so the context is $(15, 12, 9)$.

items.prose: A batch of 64 contexts of 3 looks up an embedding table of 27 by 16.
items.question: How many numbers does each joined context have?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Three lookups of 16, joined.

byKey.emb: That is one lookup; the context joins three.

explain.text: `C[X]` is (64, 3, 16); joining gives (64, 48), so 48 numbers a context.

items.prose: A model has context 2, embedding 5, 50 hidden units and 27 outputs.
items.question: How many weights does it have?

byKey.no-bias: You left out the biases, 50 and 27.

explain.text: $C$ 27 by 5, $W_1$ 10 by 50, $W_2$ 50 by 27, and biases of 50 and 27: 2,062 weights.

items.question: Why does the MLP need the tanh between its two weight matrices?

options.text: Without it the layers merge into one
To keep the logits between $-1$ and 1
options.why: The logits come after $W_2$ and are not squashed; the hidden values are.
It adds work; what it buys is a model that is not linear.

feedback.correct: Without a nonlinearity $W_1 W_2$ is one matrix.

explain.text: $(EW_1 + b_1)W_2 + b_2 = E(W_1W_2) + \dots$: one linear map. The tanh lets letters interact: without it each position adds its own fixed vote, so the effect of one letter could not depend on another.

items.prose: One context is (4, 7, 4) and the embedding has one number a symbol. The joined output’s gradient is $(0.6, 0.1, -0.25)$.
items.question: What gradient does row 4 of the table get?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Row 4 is used twice.

byKey.last: You kept the last use only.
byKey.first: You kept the first use only; both add.

explain.text: Row 4 is looked up in places one and three, so its gradient is $0.6 + (-0.25) = 0.35$.

items.prose: Batches of 128 are drawn from the 182,531 training rows.
items.question: About how many steps make one epoch?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the rows by the batch size.

byKey.rows: That is the rows; an epoch takes rows divided by the batch size steps.

explain.text: One epoch is one training set of rows: $182{,}531 / 128 = 1{,}426$ steps.

items.prose: A sweep of 1,000 steps from one start gives dev losses: 0.001 gives 3.0666, 0.01 gives 2.6407, 0.1 gives 2.4249, 0.3 gives 2.4190, 1 gives 2.4529.
items.question: Why is 0.001 so poor?

options.text: Its steps are too small to get far

options.why: Overshooting is the trouble at 1; at 0.001 the run has hardly started.

options.text: It is stuck in a bad minimum
options.why: Its loss is still falling; it is just slow.

feedback.correct: Too small to get anywhere in 1,000 steps.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare it with the larger steps.

explain.text: Each step moves the weights by the step size times the gradient, so 0.001 needs about a hundred times as many steps as 0.1. After 1,000 it is at 3.0666, close to its start of 3.30.

items.prose: Two runs with step sizes 0.1 and 0.3 end with last-minibatch losses of 2.53 and 2.29.
items.question: Is 0.3 better?

options.text: Not from this: compare dev losses

options.why: Five neighbouring batches of one run range from 2.29 to 2.68; a gap of 0.24 is well inside that.

options.text: No: a lower batch loss means overfitting
options.why: A low loss on 32 rows is mostly luck of the draw, not overfitting.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask how noisy one batch’s loss is.

explain.text: In the course run, steps 196 to 200 alone ranged from 2.29 to 2.68. Compare the step sizes on the dev loss: 2.4249 and 2.4190 after 1,000 steps.

items.prose: With a step size of 5 the course model’s first minibatch losses are 3.28, 7.93, 7.93, 13.65 and 13.67.
items.question: What is happening?

options.text: Each step overshoots: the run diverges
It is learning fast and will settle
options.why: The loss is rising, not falling; after 1,000 steps it is 44 nats.

options.text: The batches happen to be hard
options.why: Every batch gets worse in turn; the step size, not the data, is the cause.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the direction the losses move.

explain.text: A step of 5 jumps far past the bottom of the valley each time, landing higher; after 1,000 steps the dev loss is still far above the step-0.1 run's, above 30 nats. The sweep’s useful range is 0.1 to 0.3.
